papers.title: Computing Independent Sets of Size Three in Disk Graphs
papers.abstract: We study the problem of computing an independent set of size three in disk graphs, where vertices correspond to disks in the plane and two vertices are adjacent if their disks intersect. While computing a maximum independent set in disk graphs is NP-hard, the fixed-size case admits more efficient solutions. Given a set of $n$ disks, we present an algorithm to compute an independent set of size three in the disk graph and our algorithm runs in randomized expected $O^*(n^{5/3})$ time, where $O^*$ hides a factor of $n^{\epsilon}$ for an arbitrarily small $\epsilon > 0$. Our approach introduces a framework based on semi-algebraic range searching and tree-structured biclique partitions, which allows us to group pairs of disjoint disks into canonical subsets and avoid redundant computations. When the centers of the disks are in convex position, we solve the problem in $O(n \log^2 n)$ deterministic time. We also consider the case in which the disks themselves are in convex position, i.e., each disk contributes to the boundary of the convex hull of all disks, and obtain an $O(n \log^2 n)$ time algorithm for this setting as well. Our techniques for these cases are based on geometric properties of disk arrangements. In particular, they rely on new structural lemmas that reduce the problem to efficiently testing certain ordered configurations of disks. Our results improve upon the straightforward quadratic time approach and demonstrate how geometric structures and range searching techniques can be leveraged to solve fixed-size independent set problems in disk graphs more efficiently. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of independent sets of size three in disk graphs. Our results show that even this smallest nontrivial case exhibits rich structural properties, especially under convexity assumptions.

papers.title: Impatience Makes Matching NP-Hard
papers.abstract: Motivated by emerging applications such as online marketplaces and quantum switches, we study a dynamic bipartite matching model with impatient agents, where the two sides represent customers and suppliers. Agents of each type arrive according to an independent Poisson process, and the platform decides which pairs of agents to match. The agents are possibly impatient and may leave the system if not matched before their patience expires. The platform aims to maximize throughput, i.e., the number of matches per unit time. In this paper, we reveal an interesting phase transition in the computational hardness of throughput maximization. In particular, we show that approximating the optimal long-run throughput within a sufficiently small fixed relative error is NP-hard, even when all agents have rate-one exponential patience. This result implies a computational barrier to constructing near-optimal, efficiently executable matching policies that induce a matching process with fast mixing. On the other hand, when all agents on at least one side have infinite patience, we provide a simple polynomial-time algorithm that maximizes the throughput.

papers.title: When is Uniform Sampling Optimal? Coresets for Distributional Clustering
papers.abstract: Recent work [1] settled the optimal worst-case strong $\varepsilon$-coreset size for Euclidean $k$-means in unrestricted dimension at $\tilde{\Theta}(\min\{k^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-2}, k\varepsilon^{-4}\})$, showing that the natural target $\tilde{O}(k\varepsilon^{-2})$ is unattainable in general. For mixtures of $k$ isotropic Gaussian components with balanced weights and bounded scale imbalance in dimension $d\ge\log k$, we show that uniform sampling yields strong $\varepsilon$-coresets of size $\tilde{O}(k\varepsilon^{-2})$, without cluster separation. This saves a factor of $\min\{\sqrt{k},\varepsilon^{-2}\}$ over the worst-case bound, up to logarithms. For population approximation by independent, equally weighted samples, the near-linear rate is optimal up to logarithmic factors over this class. More generally, for datasets generated from an isotropic Gaussian mixture $\mu$ satisfying a mild cost-comparison assumption, uniform sampling yields strong $\varepsilon$-coresets of size $\tilde{O}((k\zeta_\mu+\pi_{\min}^{-1})\varepsilon^{-2})$, where $\pi_{\min}$ is the minimum component weight and $\zeta_\mu$ measures scale imbalance. Our proof uses a base-shift cost decomposition: one query center per component describes the base costs, and graph spanners control the sparse corrections from points switching centers. For general mixtures under cost and tail assumptions, we obtain $\tilde{O}((k\zeta_\mu+\pi_{\min}^{-1})\varepsilon^{-2}\min\{\sqrt{k},\varepsilon^{-2}\})$ samples. We also prove a matching $\tilde{\Omega}(\min\{k^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-2},k\varepsilon^{-4}\})$ lower bound for population approximation by uniform sampling from anisotropic Gaussian mixtures, even with equal weights and a shared covariance matrix. [1] Junqiu Hu, Lingxiao Huang, Jian Li, and Baoduo Xu. Tight coreset bounds for $(k, z)$-clustering in Euclidean and doubling metrics, 2026. arXiv:2610.34373.

papers.title: Exact Algorithms for Edge Deletion to Cactus
papers.abstract: We study two related problems on simple, un-directed graphs: Edge Deletion to Cactus and Spanning Tree to Cactus. Edge Deletion to Cactus has been known to be NP-hard on general graphs at least since 1988. We show improved exact algorithms for the former and a polynomial time algorithm for the latter.

papers.title: On the Price of Privacy for Language Identification and Generation
papers.abstract: Large language models train on sensitive user data, so we ask what differential privacy (DP) costs in language learning. We study private language identification and generation in the agnostic statistical setting. For identification, privacy is free: at every fixed $\varepsilon$, pure DP and $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP with $\delta\ge n^{-O(1)}$ keep the non-private rate $\exp(-r(n))$ for every $r(n)=o(n)$. For generation, the price depends on what is public. With a public witness bound, pure DP loses at most a factor $\Theta(\min\{1,\varepsilon\})$ in the exponent, and on suitable two-language collections the optimal rate is $\exp(-\Theta(\min\{1,\varepsilon\}\,n))$. Without such a bound, pure DP can lose the exponential rate itself, already for two languages: every rate $\exp(-o(n))$ stays achievable, but no exponential rate is. On these collections, $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP keeps an exponential rate if and only if $\log(1/\delta)=o(n)$. Three facts about pure DP drive the proofs. It turns a robustness margin into an exponentially small error. It obeys a private form of Le Cam's two-point bound. And it cannot see the absence of a string.

papers.title: Contrastive Identification and Generation in the Limit
papers.abstract: In identification in the limit (Gold, 1967), a learner reads positive examples and must eventually name the target hypothesis; in generation in the limit (Kleinberg and Mullainathan, 2024), it must eventually produce new positive examples. We study a weaker, relational signal: each observation is an unordered pair $\{x,y\}$ with $h(x)\neq h(y)$, such as a cannot-link constraint or a dissimilar-pair label, and the learner never learns which point is positive. All our results come from one object: a pair is valid for every member of a finite family exactly when its points lie in antipodal cells of the family's membership map. (1) For every corruption budget $k$, known or unknown, we characterize exactly the identifiable classes. Incomparable hypotheses must cover the domain and share more than $2k$ points, and Angluin's tell-tale sets must survive the loss of $2k$ points. Every unbounded budget makes any two hypotheses confusable. (2) A contrastive closure dimension characterizes uniform generation. On finite classes, generation fails exactly when a family that shares a presentation has a finite common support; on countable classes this finite condition no longer suffices. (3) On clean data the four learning criteria form a strict diamond. (4) Under corruption the order changes: some classes are identifiable from contrastive pairs under every finite budget by one algorithm, but not from positive examples with one corrupted example.

papers.title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
papers.abstract: Dantzig--Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying constraint families, and each candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, as in classical lot-sizing, network-design, and facility-location formulations. We prove that when an evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, methods that observe only bounds need of order $k^w$ evaluations to find a hidden group of $w$ families in the worst case. A prediction missing $e$ members reduces this to $\Theta(k^e)$ through a staged search that need not know $e$. The orders extend to several groups, prices, and growing evaluation costs. We study two predictors: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, which vanishes on groups whose families share no variable, and language models reading the model, verified by the staged search in JointDW. Such groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and in all 59 benchmark instances. Given the coefficients of constructed models with up to 16 families, one language model names a true group first in 249 of 252 answers. On the benchmark instances, decompositions chosen by language models from the text solve faster than those of GCG's detector.

papers.title: A PTAS for Euclidean Capacitated Vehicle Routing
papers.abstract: In the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), introduced by Dantzig and Ramser in 1959, we are given an $n$-node graph $G=(V,E)$ with metric edges costs $c(e)$, a depot $r\in V$, and an integer vehicle capacity $Q$. The goal is to find a minimum-cost collection of tours, each containing the depot and visiting at most other $Q$ nodes, such that the tours cover all the nodes. In this paper we focus on the Euclidean CVRP problem, where the nodes represent points on $\mathbb{R}^2$, and the edge costs are the respective Euclidean distances. Euclidean CVRP generalizes the classical NP-hard Euclidean TSP problem (the special case with $Q=n-1$), that admits a PTAS [Arora FOCS'96/Mitchell SODA'96]. A long-standing open problem has been generalizing the latter PTAS to Euclidean CVRP. A polynomial-time $(2+\epsilon)$-approximation for this problem follows from the PTAS for Euclidean TSP and the tour-partitioning technique for CVRP [Haimovich, Kan Math. OR'85]. This was the best known until a recent improvement of the approximation factor to slightly below 2 [Friggstad, Grandoni, Mousavi SODA'26]. There have been a series of papers presenting improved QPTASs by Das and Mathieu [SODA'10] (time $n^{\log^{O(1/\epsilon)}n}$), Jayaprakash and Salavatipour [SODA'22] (time $n^{O_{\epsilon}(\log^6 n)}$), and recently Sitters [ArXiV'25] (time $n^{O_{\epsilon}(\log\log n)}$). In this paper, we solve the mentioned long-standing open problem by presenting a PTAS for Euclidean CVRP.

papers.title: Matroid Parity Meets Vertex Splitting
papers.abstract: A vertex split replaces a vertex by two non-adjacent descendants and partitions its incident edges between them. We study exclusive $\ell$-shallow splitting, where each original vertex has at most $\ell+1$ descendants, with the aim of obtaining a forest, a pseudoforest, or a cluster graph. We consider two natural objectives: minimizing the total number of split operations and minimizing the number of original vertices that are split. Our main conceptual contribution is a connection between vertex splitting and matroid parity. For both forests and pseudoforests, we give a characterization of feasible splitting sequences that leads, via weighted linear matroid parity, to polynomial-time algorithms for minimizing the number of split vertices when $\ell=2$. These algorithms are complemented by NP-hardness for every fixed $\ell\ge3$; for pseudoforests, hardness holds even on graphs of maximum degree four. The total number of split operations behaves differently: for both sparse target classes, this objective is polynomial-time solvable for every $\ell$, using matroid intersection. For cluster graphs, both objectives admit linear-time algorithms when $\ell=1$ and are NP-hard for every fixed $\ell\ge2$. Together, these results identify how the target class, the local splitting bound, and the choice of objective determine the complexity of vertex splitting.

papers.title: Important Cuts with Logical Constraints: A Meta-Theorem for Eulerian Digraphs
papers.abstract: Important separators are a standard tool in parameterized cut algorithms. An $S$-$T$ separator is important if it is inclusion-wise minimal and no separator of at most the same size leaves a strict superset of the vertices reachable from $S$ after deletion. Their use relies on a boundedness theorem: for fixed $k$, the number of important $S$-$T$ separators of size at most $k$ is at most a constant ($4^k$ to be precise) independent of the input size, even in directed graphs, and they can be enumerated efficiently. The classical theory, however, controls only the size of the separator, not the structure of the source side cut off by it. Once the source side is required to satisfy a condition such as acyclicity, bipartiteness, or another logical property, the corresponding maximal source sides can be unbounded in general digraphs. This obstruction is fundamentally related to hardness phenomena in directed deletion problems such as Directed Odd Cycle Transversal}. Prior to this work, even in undirected graphs, boundedness of such maximal constrained source sides was known only in more specialized settings, not at the level of generality considered in our work.

papers.title: Cogirth-Strength Ratios and Matroid Rank Reduction
papers.abstract: In the rank-$p$ reduction problem, we are given a matroid with nonnegative element weights and seek a minimum-weight set of elements whose deletion lowers the rank by at least $p$. For graphic matroids, this is the minimum $(p+1)$-cut problem. Chekuri, Quanrud, and Xu developed a tree-packing algorithm for minimum $k$-cut, which relies on the fact that the minimum cut of a graph is at most twice its strength, the value of a maximum fractional packing of spanning trees. We generalize this approach from graphs to matroids. The matroid analogue of the minimum cut is the cogirth, the minimum weight of a cocircuit, and the analogue of graph strength is matroid strength, the value of a maximum fractional packing of bases. We show that if every matroid in a deletion-closed class has cogirth at most $d$ times its strength, then for every $p$, the natural linear programming relaxation of rank-$p$ reduction is within a factor of $d$ of the optimum. As a result, repeatedly deleting a minimum-weight cocircuit gives a $d$-approximation, and an optimal solution can be found deterministically in $n^{(2d-1)p+O(1)}$ time on $n$ elements. For graphs, $d=2$ and our framework specializes to the tree-packing approach. As applications, we bound the cogirth-strength ratio for two broad classes, and both bounds are tight. For quasi-graphic matroids, which include graphic, bicircular, frame, and lifted-graphic matroids, the ratio is at most $2$ for all weights, giving a $2$-approximation and an exact $n^{3p+O(1)}$-time algorithm. For $(k,\ell)$-count matroids of hypergraphs with $0\le \ell\le k$ and edge size at most $s$, the ratio is at most $ks$ under unit weights. This gives a $ks$-approximation and an exact $n^{(2ks-1)p+O(1)}$-time algorithm for unweighted rank-$p$ reduction.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for Differentially Private Cut Release
papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-time algorithm for releasing a nonnegative weighted synthetic graph under $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-edge differential privacy. Given an $n$-vertex nonnegative weighted graph $G=(V,w_G)$, the output $H=(V,w_H)$ satisfies, with probability at least $1-\beta$, simultaneously for every $S\subseteq V$, $|w_G(S,V\setminus S)-w_H(S,V\setminus S)| \le\gamma w_G(S,V\setminus S)+O\bigl((n\log n)/(\varepsilon\gamma)\bigr)$, provided that $\gamma,\varepsilon,\delta,\beta$ are at least inverse polynomial in $n$. For constant $\gamma,\varepsilon$ and $\delta=\beta=n^{-10}$, this improves the recently obtained additive error bound of $O(n\log^7 n)$ to $O(n\log n)$. We also prove a matching $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound. Our algorithm combines degree decomposition with private multiplicative weights, using a degree-sensitive semidefinite oracle to generate update proposals from single Gaussian samples. Each proposal is validated by a noisy check of its exact entropy decrease, and a joint R\'enyi analysis of sampling and validation avoids additional logarithmic losses.

papers.title: Optimal mixing of random-to-random shuffling on linear extensions
papers.abstract: Uniform sampling of linear extensions is a basic problem in randomized algorithms and the study of finite posets. We prove that the random-to-random shuffle of Ayyer, Schilling, and Thi\'ery mixes in $O(n\log n+n\log(1/\varepsilon))$ steps on every $n$-element poset, establishing their conjectured mixing order. With constant-time order queries, this gives an $\varepsilon$-approximate uniform sampler using $O(n^2(\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)))$ elementary operations after preprocessing. The proof establishes relative-entropy contraction by a factor $1-1/n$ for the promotion half-step. Consequently, the uniform extended-promotion chain has the same mixing order. We represent complete promotion scans as reflected coordinate paths in the order polytope and prove that a convex potential with gradients in the same polytope has diagonal Hessian mass at most one along each path. Applying this estimate to an optimal transport potential yields a sharp entropy factorization for every finite-entropy input. Linearization also gives the spectral-gap lower bound $(n+1)/n^2$.

papers.title: IsaGraphLib: Formally Verified Efficient Graph Algorithms in Isabelle/HOL
papers.abstract: We present a library of formally verified graph algorithms in Isabelle/HOL. The library covers the main problems of combinatorial optimisation on graphs: reachability, shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, matching, maximum flow, and minimum-cost flow. The algorithms in the library use most of the standard algorithm design techniques: graph search, greedy algorithms on matroids, dynamic programming, augmenting paths, blossom contraction, blocking flows, push-relabel, scaling, the primal-dual method, randomisation, and certificate checking. The library has adaptors between different types of graphs (directed, undirected, multigraphs), which allow results to be reused. Each algorithm is verified independently of its data structures, and the main algorithms are refined to efficient imperative implementations, from which we generate code in Standard ML, Scala, and Go. We developed parts of the library with large language models (LLMs), improved the quality of their proofs with a method based on statistics of our own proofs, and labelled which parts were developed by humans, by LLMs, or collaboratively. We perform a detailed experimental analysis of representative algorithms in our library, comparing it with state-of-the-art mainstream libraries, showing that our implementations are practical.

papers.title: Optimal Pattern-Avoidance Bounds for Binary Search Trees
papers.abstract: Self-adjusting binary search trees (BSTs) perform better than balanced BSTs if the access sequence has additional structure. For example, splay trees serve a sequential access sequence in linear time. Pattern avoidance captures regularity in an access sequence and unifies several classic examples of efficient BST access, such as deque and traversal sequences. A central question is how well a BST algorithm can exploit a pattern-avoiding access sequence. We present an online BST algorithm that serves an access sequence avoiding a permutation pattern $\pi$ in linear time, matching the information-theoretic lower bound. The algorithm does not need to know that pattern $\pi$ a priori. Our results answer an open problem asked by [Kozma 2016, Problem 44, strong variant]. Previously, the best known offline bound was optimal only for constant-size patterns [Berendsohn, Kozma, and Opler, STOC'24], and the best known online bound was superlinear [Chalermsook, Pettie, Yingchareonthawornchai, SODA'24] even for a constant-size pattern. As a corollary, our BST algorithm yields an optimal sorting algorithm for a pattern-avoiding sequence that supports online insertions. Previously, an optimal sorting algorithm was achieved using a mergesort-like approach [Opler, FOCS'24] in a batch setting. A key technique is to apply recursive split decomposition [Chalermsook, Chuzhoy, Saranurak, ToC'23] jointly in time and space, along with the Marcus-Tardos proof of the Stanley-Wilf conjecture. We show that the framework can be implemented online using $k$-finger BSTs, which is of independent interest. Finally, this framework also yields a constant-factor-approximation FPT algorithm in the offline setting.

papers.title: Tight Bounds for Non-Monotone Submodular Maximization under a Cardinality Constraint with Constant Recourse
papers.abstract: We study the maximization of a nonnegative submodular function under a cardinality constraint when elements arrive one at a time and an algorithm must report a feasible set after every arrival. The recourse of an algorithm is the largest number of insertions and deletions that it makes to the reported set at a single arrival. For every $\epsilon>0$, we give an algorithm with recourse $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ whose reported set has, at every time, expected value at least $1/4-\epsilon$ times the largest value of a feasible set of arrived elements. The algorithm evaluates the function polynomially often, and only on sets of arrived elements. We also show that no algorithm with constant recourse achieves a ratio above $1/4$, even if it knows the function and the arrival order in advance and has unlimited computation, and that any fixed ratio above $1/4$ requires recourse that grows as a positive power of the cardinality budget. Thus $1/4$ is the optimal limiting ratio with constant recourse. The previous best ratio with constant recourse was $3-2\sqrt2\approx0.172$. Our algorithm assigns selection probabilities of at most one half and maintains, as elements arrive, an inequality bounding the value of every feasible set by a multiple of the expected value of a random set drawn with these probabilities; the reported set moves to a rounding of these probabilities through gradual replacements. The upper bound uses a weighted directed graph whose vertices arrive in groups of decreasing sizes.

papers.title: Multi-seed information diffusion with varying reproduction
papers.abstract: We define the $S_hR_k$-process that generalizes the notion of Hamiltonicity through the lense of information diffusion. We say that a graph is $S_hR_k$-infectable if it can be fully infected by transmission trees seeded by at most $h$ initial infections in which each infection leads to at most $k$ others; or, equivalently, if it can be exactly vertex-covered by at most $h$ trees of degree at most $k$. While determining $S_hR_k$ infectability is NP-hard in general, we argue fixed-parameter tractability when parameterised by treewidth. Additionally, we give computational experimental results comparing the performance of several natural heuristics for minimising the number of initial infections required to an optimal LP-based approach on several standard complex network models. We find that a uniformly random approach outperforms greedy heuristics based on degree or clustering.

papers.title: Minimum Sum-of-Radii Clustering with Strong and Weak Oracles
papers.abstract: In the minimum sum of radii (MSR) problem, the input is a set of $n$ points in a metric space and a parameter $k$, and the goal is to cover the points by at most $k$ balls, each centered at an input point, while minimizing the sum of their radii. We study MSR in the weak-strong oracle model of Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram, and Wang (COLT'24), where the metric is unknown and is accessed through two oracles. The answers of the weak oracle are given to us for free: for every pair of points, we receive a distance value that, with probability $\delta$, is arbitrarily corrupted. Exact distances are available only through costly strong queries, where a strong query on a point reveals its exact distances to all previously strongly queried points, and the goal is to minimize the number of strong queries. For every constant $\delta < 1/2$, we give the first polynomial-time algorithm that makes $O(k \log n \log\log n)$ strong point queries and, with high probability, returns an $O(1)$-approximation for MSR; the previously best algorithm required running time and a number of strong queries exponential in $k$. This is within an $O(\log\log n)$ factor of a lower bound that we prove: any constant-factor approximation that succeeds with high probability on every instance must make $\Omega(k \log n)$ strong queries in expectation on some instance. The same $\Omega(k \log n)$ lower bound holds for $k$-center, where it matches the known upper bound up to an $O(\log\log n)$ factor. An optimal MSR cluster can be small both in size and in radius, so a uniform sample of strongly queried points may miss it entirely. Instead, our algorithm uses a packing LP over the balls certified so far to decide which points to query next. The analysis holds against an adversary who knows which pairs are corrupted.

papers.title: Online and Fully-Dynamic Sorting
papers.abstract: Online sorting asks how to place $n$ sequentially arriving elements in an array to minimize the sum of absolute differences between consecutive elements. Fully-dynamic sorting further extends the problem to allow both element insertions and deletions. Without recourse, these problems face strong lower bounds on the competitive ratio: $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for online sorting and $\Omega(n)$ for fully-dynamic sorting. In sharp contrast, we show that allowing only poly-logarithmic recourse yields at least exponential improvements in the competitive ratio for both problems:(1) Our main algorithmic result is a deterministic fully-dynamic sorting algorithm that is $O(\log^2 n)$-competitive and has $O(\log^4 n)$ amortized recourse per update. We complement this with a lower bound showing that any deterministic algorithm with any $O(\mathrm{polylog}(n))$ competitive ratio has amortized recourse at least $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$.(2) For the insertion-only setting, we establish a family of approximation--recourse tradeoffs, including $O(\log\log n)$ competitive ratio with $O(\log\log n)$ amortized recourse. Given the lower bound in the fully-dynamic case, this result shows that the insertion-only problem yields exponentially better bounds than the fully-dynamic one.(3) Finally, we show that the stronger approximation-recourse tradeoff for the insertion-only case extends to the fully-dynamic setting when the array has $(1+\varepsilon)n$ space.

papers.title: Rounded Potentials Certify Exact Maximum Flow
papers.abstract: The textbook certificate for maximum flow is lopsided: the cut takes one bit per vertex, while the flow takes one number per edge. Indeed, some graphs have $\Theta(n^2)$ terminal pairs for which every maximum flow uses $\Theta(n^2)$ edges. Yet we show that one short number per vertex suffices for both cut and flow: $n$ vertex potentials, each rounded to $O(\log(nW))$ bits, certify the exact maximum $st$-flow value in any directed graph with integer capacities at most $W$. Exact potentials can have exponentially large representations. Rounding them may violate flow conservation, but the total error across any cut is less than one unit, so integrality of cut capacities absorbs it. Checking conservation is local and linear in the capacities, allowing the same certificate to yield new bounds in four models (capacities are polynomially bounded unless stated otherwise): - Online annotated streaming. $\widetilde{O}(n)$ total cost (help plus space) for the maximum $st$-flow value, optimal up to logarithmic factors, answering a question of Thaler (ICALP 2016) on whether $o(n^2)$ is possible. - Broadcast proof-labeling. $O(\log(n+p))$-bit labels certifying a maximum $st$-flow value of $p$ in directed and undirected graphs with arbitrary capacities, optimal for $p\ge n^{\Omega(1)}$, settling that regime of a question of Korman, Kutten, and Peleg (Distributed Computing 2010). - Merlin-Arthur verification. $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ time and $O(n^3\log n)$ proof length for directed All-Pairs Max-Flow, improving on previous verification times of $n^{4+o(1)}$ for general capacities and $n^{3.5+o(1)}$ for unit capacities, and answering a question of Akmal (TheoretiCS 2024). - Nondeterministic algorithms. $O(n^{3.614})$ time for directed All-Pairs Max-Flow, or $n^{3.5+o(1)}$ if $\omega=2$: the first subquartic bound for general edge capacities, answering a question of Trabelsi (SODA 2025).

papers.title: Improved Approximation for Weighted $k$-Set Packing via a Simple Two-Phase Approach
papers.abstract: Weighted $k$-set packing asks for a maximum-weight collection of pairwise disjoint sets, each of cardinality at most $k$. For every fixed $k\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm with approximation factor $\left(1- 1/{\sqrt3} \right)k+O(\log k) \approx 0.4226k + O(\log k)$, improving the previous best factor of $0.4621k + O(\sqrt{k})$ through a simple two-phase approach. In a first phase, our algorithm constructs a packing by processing random weight buckets of varying widths with an unweighted packing algorithm. We show that a small expected weight of this packing relative to the optimum forces a large expected total surplus in the optimum. Surplus quantifies the potential for improving a packing through star swaps. In the second phase, we solve and round a configuration LP to turn sufficiently large surplus into an increase in expected weight. Our procedure can easily be derandomized.

papers.title: Speed-Robust Scheduling for Total Completion Time
papers.abstract: We study two-stage speed-robust scheduling for minimizing total completion time. Jobs must be partitioned into $M$ bags before an adversary reveals the speeds of at most $M$ machines. Each bag is then assigned to one available machine, and the jobs on each machine may be processed in any order independent of the bags. We compare with an optimal schedule that knows the speeds in advance and assigns jobs individually. This model has been studied for makespan minimization. We initiate its study for total completion time, as suggested by Stein and Zhong (TALG 2020). For an unknown number of identical machines, we show that the optimal deterministic robustness factor is exactly~$13/12$, both for unit-size jobs and for arbitrary processing times. For infinitesimally small jobs, the factor lies between $31/30\approx1.0333$ and $28/27\approx1.0370$, well below the optimal makespan factor of about $1.2071$. General speeds make the problem strictly harder: no deterministic algorithm is better than $1.2669$-robust, already for infinitesimally small jobs. We give a $25/16$-robust algorithm for arbitrary processing times and improve the guarantee to $1681/1152\approx1.4592$ for infinitesimally small jobs. Our main tools are a layer decomposition that extends guarantees from unit-size jobs to arbitrary processing times when one assignment satisfies them for every prefix in non-increasing processing-time order, and a threshold analysis of the bag counts produced by greedy assignment rules.

papers.title: Copying along Arithmetic Progressions Cannot Simulate Interleaving with Polylogarithmic Loss
papers.abstract: Two classical ways to compress a word are straight-line programs (SLPs), which build it by concatenating smaller pieces, and the Lempel-Ziv 77 (LZ77) factorisation, which copies earlier parts of it; their sizes are measures of repetitiveness. LZ77 approximates the smallest SLP efficiently: it has no more factors than a smallest SLP has size, and yields an SLP at most a logarithmic factor larger in near-linear time. Motivated by online prediction, Kosoy introduced zipline programs, which are analogous to SLPs but interleave their pieces round-robin instead of concatenating them. Her generalisation of LZ77, the arithmetic repetition system, describes a word by copies from one arithmetic progression of positions to a later one. Do arithmetic repetition systems approximate the smallest zipline program as well? Kosoy proved that the least size $\mathrm{ARC}(x)$ of an arithmetic repetition system for a word $x$ of length $n$ is at most a factor $O(n^{1/3})$ larger than the least size $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ of a zipline program for it, and asked whether this factor is tight. Her polynomial-time next-letter predictor makes $O(\mathrm{ARC}(x)\log n)$ mistakes, so a polylogarithmic factor would bound its mistakes by $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$, which no known polynomial-time predictor achieves. We show that the optimal exponent is $1/4$, not $1/3$: $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \le 2n^{1/4}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ for every word $x$, and at every large enough length $n$ some binary word has $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \ge n^{1/4-o(1)}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$.

papers.title: Subexponential algorithms for structural parameterizations of Vertex Cover in geometric graphs
papers.abstract: A number of recent works have investigated the existence of parameterized subexponential algorithms in geometric graph classes for hitting a fixed small graph as a subgraph or as a minor. In this setting, given an $n$-vertex graph, the goal is to decide in time $n^{O(1)}2^{o(k)}$ if a solution of size at most $k$ exists. Inspired by recent results in kernelization for structural parameters, we investigate subexponential algorithms for the Vertex Cover (VC) problem, but parameterized by distance-to-triviality instead of solution size. More formally, given a fixed "trivial" graph class $\mathcal{C}$, the problem takes as input $(G,X,k)$, where $G \setminus X \in \mathcal{C}$, and asks if $G$ admits a vertex cover of size at most $k$. Our goal is to design algorithms for this problem running in time $n^{O(1)}2^{o(|X|)}$. The motivation is that, since $|X|$ is typically arbitrarily smaller than $k$, such algorithms might be faster than ETH-tight subexponential algorithms parameterized by $k$. We identify two sets of sufficient conditions under which the problem admits a subexponential algorithm: one for the case where $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of paths, and another for the case where $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of graphs of constant treedepth. We also provide two applications of these algorithmic results: we prove that $s$-string graphs and pseudo-disk graphs satisfy the first set of conditions, whereas string graphs satisfy the second set. The two sets share a common condition that might be of independent interest, as it implies a property that bounds the treewidth of any string graph in terms of a given modulator to a fixed graph class $\mathcal{C}$. Finally, concerning more restricted graph classes having the $ASQGM(\omega)$ property (such as map graphs and $H$-minor free graphs), we prove a dichotomy, depending on the maximum treewidth in $\mathcal{C}$.

papers.title: Path-constrained Packing on Trees
papers.abstract: An instance of Budgeted Path-constrained Packing on Trees (BPPT) consists of a graph $G$ together with a spanning tree $T$, a weight $w_e \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ for each tree edge $e \in E(T)$ and a budget $b_f \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$ for each non-tree edge $f \in E(G) \setminus E(T)$. The goal is to find a maximum weight packing of fundamental cuts respecting the budgets. Equivalently, an instance of BPPT is an integer program of the form $\max \{w^\intercal x : Ax \le b,\ x \in \{0,1\}^n\}$ where $A \in \{0,1\}^{m \times n}$ is a transposed edge-path-tree matrix, $w \in \mathbb{Z}^n_{\ge 0}$ and $b \in \mathbb{Z}^m_{\ge 1}$. We define the congestion $C$ of a BPPT instance as the maximum number of non-zeros in a column of $A$. The unit congestion $UC$ is defined similarly, except that rows with $b_i \ge 2$ are ignored. We also consider the minimum budget $\beta := \min \{b_i : i = 1, \ldots, m\}$. In this paper, we begin the study of BPPT through the lens of the three parameters $C$, $UC$ and $\beta$, and relative to the standard LP relaxation $\max \{w^\intercal x : Ax \le b,\ x \in [0,1]^n\}$. BPPT generalizes the independent set problem in graphs of maximum degree at most $C$ and is a special case of the $b$-matching problem in hypergraphs of rank at most $C$. We obtain approximation algorithms for BPPT with factors $2+UC/2$, $1+C/2$ and $\beta/(\beta-1)$ for $\beta \geq 2$. These bounds are relative to the standard LP relaxation and, as we show, integrality gap tight with respect to parameters $UC$ and $\beta$, and almost integrality gap tight relative to $C$. We complement these results with a $\lceil (C+1)/3 \rceil$-approximation for fixed $C$ which is not relative to the standard LP relaxation and has $\textsf{XP}$ running time parameterized by $C$.

papers.title: An Optimal Online Algorithm for Single-machine Scheduling with Two Agents
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the online two-agent scheduling problem on a single machine, where jobs arrive over time. The objective is to minimize the weighted sum of the agents' makespans, denoted as $C_{\max}^A + \theta C_{\max}^B$, for a given priority weight $\theta \ge 1$. A significant gap has persisted between the established theoretical lower bound on the competitive ratio and the performance of the best-known online algorithms. For the parameter range $1 \leq \theta \leq \tfrac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$, we propose novel online algorithm which achieves a competitive ratio of $1+\tfrac{\theta}{1+\theta}$. This result matches the theoretical lower bound.

papers.title: A Polynomial Time Algorithm for Finding a Minimum 5-Partition of a Submodular Function
papers.abstract: Given a real-valued submodular function on a finite ground set, the minimum $k$-partition problem asks for a partition into $k$ nonempty parts minimizing the sum of their function values. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for $k=5$. The idea follows directly from the previous $k=4$ result, where there is precisely one obstruction for generalizing it to $k=5$. We show the special case can be handled by reasoning about a restricted family of $3$-partitions.

papers.title: Constant-Factor Matching-Size Estimation in Random-Order Streams
papers.abstract: We give a one-pass algorithm that estimates the maximum matching size of an arbitrary simple graph within a constant factor using $O(\log^2 n)$ bits of space. The edges arrive exactly once in uniformly random order. The algorithm succeeds with probability at least $2/3$, does not require the number of edges in advance, and has worst-case total running time $O((m+1)\log(n+2))$ on a word RAM. Kapralov, Khanna, and Sudan (SODA 2014) obtained a polylogarithmic approximation in polylogarithmic space. Kapralov, Mitrovi\'c, Norouzi-Fard, and Tardos (SODA 2020) subsequently gave a constant-factor approximation from independent uniform edge samples and an $O(\log^2 n)$-approximation in random order. We obtain a constant factor in the latter model with the same $O(\log^2 n)$ space bound. The main ingredient is a comparison between the memory states of a recursive sampling algorithm under sampling with and without replacement. We account jointly for the sampled edges retained by the recursion and the positions at which they arrived. Randomized thresholds limit the additional information stored in numerical counters. A bound on the expected work of the entire recursion then removes the loss from its logarithmic depth. The resulting estimator repeatedly improves a coarse estimate while storing only one recursion stack.

papers.title: Reducing Asymmetric Path TSP to Asymmetric TSP
papers.abstract: In the Asymmetric Traveling Salesman Problem (Asymmetric TSP), we are given distances between $n$ vertices that satisfy the triangle inequality but need not be symmetric, and we seek a shortest tour through all vertices. In its path version, Asymmetric Path TSP, two vertices $s$ and $t$ are prescribed, and we seek a shortest path from $s$ to $t$ through all vertices. Both problems are equivalent to their versions with arbitrary nonnegative edge costs on a directed graph, in which vertices may be visited more than once. We show that for all constants $\alpha\ge1$ and $\varepsilon>0$, any $\alpha$-approximation algorithm for Asymmetric TSP yields an $(\alpha+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for Asymmetric Path TSP. The best previous reduction of this kind, due to Feige and Singh, yields an $\alpha(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm. Our result answers an open question of Traub and Vygen. Consequently, every constant-factor approximation guarantee for Asymmetric TSP carries over to Asymmetric Path TSP up to an arbitrarily small additive error.

papers.title: Associahedra are 8-colourable
papers.abstract: Determining the chromatic number of associahedra is a long-standing open problem. Tan [arXiv:2611.05323] recently proved that associahedra are 12-colourable, which is the first constant upper bound. This paper adapts Tan's argument to show that associahedra are 8-colourable.
